etymology: From the Latin stipula, “a stalk,” the short, dry stalks of grain left standing in the field after the harvest is reaped.
biblical_def: Stubble is the dry, worthless residue of the harvest — the short stalks left in the field when the grain is gathered, fit for nothing but to be burned or driven before the wind. In Scripture it is the steady image of the wicked and their works under the judgment of God. Job declares of the ungodly, “They are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away” (Job 21:18), for the prosperity of the wicked is light and rootless, swept off in a moment. The prophet Malachi sets the same image at the last day: “Behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up” (Mal 4:1). Paul takes up the figure for the works of professing men: the wood, hay, and stubble built upon the foundation shall be tried by fire and consumed, though the builder himself, if he be in Christ, is saved (1Co 3:12–15). Yet stubble was not in itself contemptible, for Israel in Egypt was made to gather stubble for straw to make their bricks (Exo 5:12). The word teaches that whatever is dry, rootless, and apart from God’s life cannot stand the fire of His judgment, but is driven away and burned up in the day of the LORD.
webster_summary: The dry stalks left after harvest; in Scripture the image of the wicked and their works, driven before the wind and burned in judgment.

corruption_summary: An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the wicked and their rootless works are burned up in the judgment of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of judgment upon all that is rootless and ungodly. Stubble is the dry remnant of the harvest, fit only for the fire; and so the LORD by it teaches that the prosperity of the wicked is light and momentary, swept off like chaff before the storm. The day cometh that shall burn as an oven, and all that do wickedly shall be stubble before it. Whatever is not rooted in the life of God cannot endure His holy fire.

The figure also searches the works of professing men, for Paul warns that wood, hay, and stubble built upon the true foundation shall be burned in the day of trial, though the builder himself, if he be in Christ, is saved yet so as by fire. The lesson is that men must build with gold and silver and precious stones — that is, with the enduring work of faith — and not with the dry stubble of self-will and vanity that the fire of God will consume.

etymology: An old English word for the noxious weed darnel, a grass that closely resembles wheat in the blade but is worthless and noxious when grown.
biblical_def: Tares are the weed darnel, a poisonous grass that springs up among the wheat and so resembles it in the early blade that the two cannot safely be told apart until the ear appears. Our Lord made the tares the matter of one of His kingdom parables: “The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field: but while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way” (Mat 13:24–25). When the servants would gather up the tares, the householder forbade them, lest in rooting up the tares they root up the wheat also, and bade them let both grow together until the harvest (Mat 13:30). The Lord Himself interpreted the parable: the good seed are the children of the kingdom; the tares are the children of the wicked one; the enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels (Mat 13:38–39). At that harvest the tares are bound in bundles to be burned, and the wheat is gathered into the barn. The parable teaches that the visible church and the world contain a mingled crop of the righteous and the wicked, sown together and growing together, which the Lord will not separate before the appointed day. It rebukes the impatience that would purge the field by human violence, and it sets the final, certain separation in the hand of God at the end of the world.
webster_summary: The weed darnel sown among the wheat by the enemy; in the Lord’s parable the children of the wicked one, separated and burned at the harvest.

corruption_summary: A parable-image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the righteous and the wicked grow together until God separates them at the harvest.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Lord’s own teaching that the field of this world holds a mingled crop, the children of the kingdom and the children of the wicked one, sown together by God and by the enemy, and growing together until the harvest. The tares so resemble the wheat that men cannot infallibly part them now; and the householder forbids the servants to pluck them up, lest they harm the wheat. The lesson is patience under the present mingling, and confidence that the LORD will make the final separation in His own day.

The parable rebukes two opposite errors. It rebukes the impatience that would purge the visible church by human violence, tearing up supposed tares and harming true wheat in the process; for the separation belongs to the angels at the end of the world, not to the servants now. And it rebukes the carelessness that denies any separation at all, for the tares shall surely be bound in bundles and burned, and the wheat gathered into the barn. The harvest is certain, and the Judge is God.

etymology: From wine and the old word fat, a vat or trough; the lower vessel of a winepress into which the trodden juice of the grapes ran down.
biblical_def: A winefat, or wine-vat, was the lower trough hewn beneath the winepress, into which the juice of the grapes flowed when they were trodden out by the feet of the labourers. It was a familiar part of every well-ordered vineyard, and our Lord set it in the parable of the householder: “A certain man planted a vineyard, and set an hedge about it, and digged a place for the winefat, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country” (Mar 12:1). The vineyard there is the house of Israel, hedged, furnished, and entrusted to husbandmen who would not render the fruit, and who slew at last the heir himself; the digging of the winefat marks the completeness of the LORD’s provision and care for His vineyard. But the treading of the winepress is also throughout Scripture a sober type of the wrath of God against His enemies. Isaiah sees the LORD coming from Edom with dyed garments, and asks, “Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat?” (Isa 63:2); and the answer is, “I have trodden the winepress alone” (Isa 63:3), for the LORD treads down the nations in His anger as grapes are trodden in the press. The winefat thus joins two solemn truths: the fulness of God’s gracious provision for His vineyard, and the terror of His judgment, when the wicked are trodden in the great winepress of His wrath.
webster_summary: The trough beneath a winepress that received the trodden juice; figure of God’s provision for His vineyard and of the treading of His wrath.

corruption_summary: An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses both God’s full provision for His vineyard and the treading of His wrath.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. First, the digged winefat in the Lord’s parable shows the completeness of God’s gracious provision for His vineyard: He set the hedge, digged the winefat, built the tower, and lacked nothing in His care, so that the unfruitfulness of the husbandmen was wholly without excuse. The lesson is the great guilt of those who, entrusted with every mercy, will not render the fruit unto the Lord of the vineyard.

Second, the treading of the winefat is the steady scriptural type of the wrath of God. Isaiah sees the LORD red in His apparel, like one who has trodden grapes, and the answer is that He has trodden the winepress of judgment alone, trampling the nations in His fury. The figure that elsewhere speaks of harvest gladness is here turned to terror, and warns that the same God who provides so fully for His vineyard will tread the wicked in the winepress of His holy anger.

etymology: From the Old English sceaf, a bundle; the cut stalks of grain bound together in the field at the harvest.
biblical_def: A sheaf is a bundle of cut grain, bound together as the reapers gather the harvest. The word carries a rich thread of meaning through Scripture, from dreams and firstfruits to the sure reward of those who sow in tears. Joseph dreamed of sheaves in the field: “For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf” (Gen 37:7), a dream that foretold his exaltation over his brethren. Under the law, the first sheaf of the harvest was waved before the LORD as the firstfruits: “then ye shall bring a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest unto the priest” (Lev 23:10), and the priest waved it on the morrow after the sabbath (Lev 23:11). This wave sheaf, the firstfruits of the barley harvest, was a type fulfilled in Christ, who is risen from the dead and become the firstfruits of them that slept, the first sheaf of the great resurrection harvest. And the Psalmist makes the sheaf the emblem of the reward of faithful, sorrowful labour: “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him” (Psa 126:6). The sheaf thus gathers up the providence that exalts the lowly, the firstfruits that consecrate the whole, and the harvest joy that crowns the sowing of tears.
webster_summary: A bound bundle of cut grain; emblem of Joseph’s exaltation, the firstfruits waved before the LORD, and the joyful reward of those who sow in tears.

corruption_summary: An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses providence, the firstfruits consecrated to God, and the harvest joy that crowns sowing in tears.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the consecration of the firstfruits, for the law commanded that the first sheaf of the harvest be waved before the LORD before the people might eat of their increase. This wave sheaf was a type fulfilled in Christ, who is risen as the firstfruits of them that slept, the first sheaf of the great resurrection harvest; and it teaches still that God must have the first and the best, the whole lump being sanctified by the firstfruits offered unto Him.

The sheaf also carries the sweet promise of harvest joy to those who labour in sorrow. “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.” The seed sown in tears is not lost; the LORD watches over it, and the weeping sower is brought home at last laden with sheaves. So the faithful are taught that present sorrow in the Lord’s work shall ripen into a sure and joyful harvest.

etymology: From the Greek mandragoras; a fragrant plant of the nightshade kind bearing yellow fruit, anciently reckoned a token of love and fruitfulness.
biblical_def: Mandrakes are the fruit of a low plant of the nightshade kind, sweet-smelling and golden, which ripened about the time of the wheat harvest and was anciently reputed among the nations to be a love-token and a help to fruitfulness. They come into the sacred story in the contention between Leah and Rachel, the wives of Jacob. “Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah” (Gen 30:14). Rachel, who was barren and envied her sister’s children, begged the mandrakes of Leah, and bought them with the price of Jacob’s company for a night; and so Leah conceived again (Gen 30:14–16). The passage shows the household of the patriarch entangled in rivalry, superstition, and the longing for children, and yet the LORD overruling all to build the house of Israel through the twelve sons He had purposed to give. It is God, not the mandrakes, who opens and shuts the womb; for it was Leah, who had the mandrakes and bartered them away, that conceived, while Rachel remained barren until God remembered her and Himself opened her womb (Gen 30:22). The mandrakes appear again among the delights of the garden in the Song of Solomon: “the mandrakes give a smell” (Son 7:13), a fragrant emblem of the fruitful love of the bridegroom and the bride. The plant thus stands at the meeting of human longing and divine providence, a reminder that the gift of children is from the LORD alone.
webster_summary: A fragrant nightshade plant reputed a love-token; the fruit Reuben gathered, over which Leah and Rachel contended, though God alone opens the womb.

corruption_summary: An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the gift of children is from the LORD alone, not from charms or means.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD alone opens and shuts the womb, and that no plant or charm can supply what He withholds or accomplish what He has not purposed. The mandrakes were anciently reputed to aid fruitfulness, and Rachel coveted them in her barrenness; yet it was Leah, who bartered the mandrakes away, who conceived, while Rachel remained barren until God remembered her and Himself opened her womb. The narrative quietly rebukes the trust in means and tokens and exalts the providence of God over the building of His people.

The history also lays bare the rivalry and superstition that troubled even the household of the patriarch, and shows the LORD overruling such weakness to His own gracious ends. Out of the contention of Leah and Rachel God built the twelve tribes of Israel, fulfilling His covenant purpose through the tangled affections of men. The mandrakes that perfume the garden in the Song remind us that fruitfulness and conjugal love are good gifts of God, to be received from His hand and not sought by the devices of the heathen.

etymology: From the Old French gourde; a quick-growing, broad-leaved trailing plant, used in Jonah’s history of a vine that God prepared and smote in a night.
biblical_def: A gourd is a broad-leaved, quick-growing plant of the trailing or climbing kind, whose spreading foliage gives a grateful shade. The most famous gourd of Scripture is the one God prepared over Jonah. When the prophet, angry that Nineveh was spared, sat without the city to see what would become of it, “the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head, to deliver him from his grief. So Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd” (Jon 4:6). But God prepared also a worm that smote the gourd so that it withered, and a vehement east wind, until Jonah fainted and wished to die (Jon 4:7–8). Then the LORD reasoned with His servant: “Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow” (Jon 4:10), and should not God spare great Nineveh, with its multitude of souls? The gourd thus became a living parable of God’s tender care for His creatures and of the narrowness of the prophet’s heart, which pitied a withered weed yet grudged mercy to a city. A different gourd appears in the school of the prophets, where wild gourds were shred into the pot and made the pottage deadly until Elisha healed it (2Ki 4:39–40). The gourd teaches that God prepares and removes the comforts of His people at His will, and that His compassion reaches far beyond their own.

corruption_summary: An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses God’s providence over the comforts of His people and the breadth of His mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the comforts of His people. The LORD prepared the gourd to shade Jonah, and the LORD prepared the worm that smote it; the comfort came up in a night and perished in a night, wholly at His appointment. The lesson is that the shadows under which we sit are God’s gift, given and taken at His will, and that the heart must not cling to the gourd as though it were its own labour or its lasting portion.

The gourd is also a mirror held up to the narrowness of the prophet’s heart, and so to ours. Jonah pitied a withered weed for which he had not laboured, yet grudged mercy to a great city of perishing souls. The LORD’s gentle reasoning — should not He spare Nineveh, with its multitude that knew not their right hand from their left? — rebukes every spirit that prizes its own ease above the mercy of God toward sinners. The compassion of God reaches far beyond the small affections of His servants.

etymology: From the Old English netele; a stinging weed that springs up in waste and neglected ground, an emblem of desolation and judgment.
biblical_def: The nettle is a coarse, stinging weed that springs up in waste places, ruined fields, and neglected ground, and so became in Scripture a steady emblem of desolation, slothfulness, and the judgment of God. The wise man, passing the field of the slothful and the vineyard of the man void of understanding, saw that “it was all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof, and the stone wall thereof was broken down” (Pro 24:31), and he took instruction from the sight against idleness. The prophets make the nettle the very mark of a land laid waste under the wrath of God. Zephaniah foretells of Moab and Ammon that they shall be “the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation” (Zep 2:9). Hosea warns rebellious Israel that “the pleasant places for their silver, nettles shall possess them: thorns shall be in their tabernacles” (Hos 9:6). And Job, in his abasement, describes the basest of men, driven out from among the living, who “among the bushes they brayed; under the nettles they were gathered together” (Job 30:7). Wherever the nettle spreads, the hand of man has failed and the curse has come in: the wall broken, the field forsaken, the dwelling emptied. The nettle preaches the bitter fruit of sloth and the desolation that follows the judgment of God, that what was once pleasant and fruitful becomes a thicket of stinging weeds.
webster_summary: A stinging weed of waste and neglected ground; emblem of the slothful’s ruin and of the desolation that follows the judgment of God.

corruption_summary: An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses the bitter fruit of sloth and the desolation that follows the judgment of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the desolation that sloth and sin bring upon a land. The wise man looked upon the field of the slothful and saw it grown over with thorns and covered with nettles, the wall broken down; and he received instruction against idleness. The nettle preaches that what is neglected does not stay empty but is overrun with stinging weeds, and that the ruin of the careless is the certain harvest of their sloth.

More solemnly, the prophets make the nettle the mark of a land laid waste under the judgment of God. Where the wrath of God has come in, the pleasant places are possessed by nettles, and the dwellings filled with thorns; Moab and Ammon become a breeding of nettles and a perpetual desolation. The weed that springs in ruined ground thus preaches the bitter end of rebellion against the LORD, when the fruitful field He gave is turned to a thicket of desolation.

roots_lines: Nettle — from Old English netele.
A coarse, stinging weed of waste and neglected ground.
It covered the field of the slothful (Pro 24:31).
It marks lands laid waste under judgment (Zep 2:9; Hos 9:6).
The basest of men gather under it in their abasement (Job 30:7).
usage: Like the nettle over the slothful’s field, what is neglected is overrun with stinging weeds.
The nettle teaches that ruin is the certain harvest of idleness and careless ground.
Where the prophets see nettles spread, the judgment of God has turned the pleasant place to desolation.

etymology: From the Old English brær; a prickly, thorny shrub, emblem of the curse and of the grieving of God’s people, set against the myrtle in promises of restoration.
biblical_def: A brier is a prickly, thorny shrub that springs up in cursed and neglected ground, and in Scripture it stands as an emblem of the curse, of grief, and of judgment — yet one which the LORD promises to reverse in the day of His mercy. Briers and thorns came in with the curse upon the ground for man’s sin, and the prophets often join them as the mark of desolation. But the brightest use of the brier is in the great promise of restoration: “Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off” (Isa 55:13). Here the curse itself is turned to blessing, the thorny waste giving place to the fragrant myrtle, as a sign of the new covenant work of God in His people. Ezekiel comforts the house of Israel that there shall be “no more a pricking brier unto the house of Israel, nor any grieving thorn of all that are round about them, that despised them” (Eze 28:24), for the LORD will remove the malice of their enemies. And Micah laments the corruption of the age: “the best of them is as a brier: the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge” (Mic 7:4), where even the righteous-seeming wound those near them. The brier thus marks the curse and the grief that sin has brought, and shines most brightly as the very thing the LORD removes when He plants the myrtle in its place.
webster_summary: A thorny shrub, emblem of the curse and of grief; the very thing God reverses when He plants the myrtle in its place (Isa 55:13).
webster_full: BRIER, a prickly, thorny shrub of cursed ground.
Instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree (Isa 55:13).
There shall be no more a pricking brier to Israel (Eze 28:24).
The best of a corrupt people is as a brier (Mic 7:4).
It is an emblem of the curse and of grief turned to blessing.
scriptures: Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off.
And there shall be no more a pricking brier unto the house of Israel, nor any grieving thorn of all that are round about them, that despised them; and they shall know that I am the Lord GOD.

Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briers; yea, upon all the houses of joy in the joyous city:
corruption_summary: An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses the curse and grief of sin, and the mercy of God who plants the myrtle in the brier’s place.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reversal of the curse by the gracious work of God. The brier is the thorny fruit of the ground cursed for man’s sin, an emblem of grief and desolation; but the great promise of Isaiah is that “instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree.” The LORD does not merely clear the brier away but plants the fragrant myrtle in its very place, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off. The curse itself becomes the soil of blessing where God works His new-covenant mercy.

The brier also teaches the grief that sin brings among men, for Micah laments that in a corrupt generation “the best of them is as a brier,” wounding even those nearest them. And Ezekiel promises that the pricking brier and grieving thorn of Israel’s despising enemies shall be no more. So the brier marks both the wounding of God’s people in this fallen world and the sure promise that the LORD will at last remove every grief and replant His vineyard with the trees of His own planting.
roots_summary: From the Old English brær; a thorny shrub of the curse, replaced by the myrtle in the promise of God.
roots_lines: Brier — from Old English brær.
A prickly, thorny shrub of cursed and waste ground.
Instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree (Isa 55:13).
No more a pricking brier shall be to Israel (Eze 28:24).
The best of a corrupt people is as a brier (Mic 7:4).
usage: Like the brier replaced by the myrtle, God turns the very ground of the curse into the soil of blessing.
The brier teaches the grief sin brings among men, where even the best may wound those near them.
The promise of no more a pricking brier assures the saints that God will remove their every grief.

etymology: From the Greek myrtos; a fragrant evergreen shrub of the Holy Land, emblem of God’s blessing, peace, and the restoration of His people.
biblical_def: The myrtle is a fragrant evergreen shrub, dark and glossy of leaf, bearing sweet-smelling white flowers, native to the hills of the Holy Land. In Scripture it is a steady emblem of God’s blessing, peace, and the restoration of His people from desolation. In the great promise of the wilderness made glad, the LORD declares, “I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree” (Isa 41:19); and again, “instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off” (Isa 55:13), where the fragrant myrtle replaces the thorny brier of the curse. In the night vision of Zechariah, the angel of the LORD stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom (Zec 1:8–11), and the myrtles, lowly yet evergreen, picture the church of God, hidden in the valley yet kept fresh and fragrant under His watch in a day of small things. After the return from captivity, the people were commanded to fetch myrtle branches with olive and palm to make booths for the feast of tabernacles (Neh 8:15), that the joy of restored worship might be crowned with the myrtle of peace. The Hebrew name of the myrtle, Hadassah, was the very name of Esther (Est 2:7), the lowly captive maiden whom God raised to deliver His people. The myrtle thus breathes the fragrance of God’s covenant mercy, the lowly and evergreen beauty of His preserved church.
webster_summary: A fragrant evergreen shrub; emblem of God’s blessing and the restoration of His people, the myrtle of Zechariah’s vision and the name of Esther.
webster_full: MYRTLE TREE, a fragrant evergreen shrub of the Holy Land.
The LORD plants it in the wilderness made glad (Isa 41:19).
Instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree (Isa 55:13).
The angel stood among the myrtle trees in the bottom (Zec 1:8).
Its Hebrew name, Hadassah, was the name of Esther (Est 2:7).

corruption_summary: An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses God’s blessing, the restoration of His people, and the lowly evergreen beauty of His church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD’s blessing that turns the desolate place into a garden. He plants the myrtle in the wilderness, and sets it in the place of the brier, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off. The fragrant evergreen replacing the thorny weed is a figure of the new-covenant mercy of God, who does not merely clear away the curse but plants the trees of His own glory where the brier once stood, that His restored people may flourish before Him.

The myrtle also pictures the lowly and preserved church of God. In Zechariah’s vision the angel of the LORD stood among the myrtle trees in the bottom — lowly shrubs in a shaded valley, yet evergreen and fragrant under His watchful eye in a day of small things. And the Hebrew name of the myrtle, Hadassah, was borne by Esther, the captive maiden God exalted to save His people. So the myrtle breathes the fragrance of God’s faithful care over a church that seems hidden and small, yet is kept fresh and fruitful by His covenant love.
roots_summary: From the Greek myrtos; a fragrant evergreen shrub, emblem of blessing and restoration, whose Hebrew name Hadassah was Esther’s.
roots_lines: Myrtle Tree — from Greek myrtos.
A fragrant evergreen shrub of the Holy Land.
The LORD plants it in the wilderness made glad (Isa 41:19).
It replaces the brier of the curse (Isa 55:13).
Its Hebrew name Hadassah was the name of Esther (Est 2:7).
usage: Like the myrtle set in the brier’s place, God plants His blessing where the curse once reigned.
The myrtle of Zechariah’s valley pictures the lowly church kept evergreen under the LORD’s watch.
Hadassah the myrtle, who was Esther, shows God exalting the lowly to deliver His people.

etymology: From the Old English spearwa; small common birds of little worth in the market, made by our Lord the emblem of the Father’s particular care.
biblical_def: Sparrows are small, common birds, so little esteemed that two were sold for a farthing and five for two farthings in the markets of Galilee. Our Lord took up this cheapest of creatures to teach the most tender truth of the Father’s providence over His people: “Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows” (Mat 10:29–31). Luke gives the saying with five sparrows sold for two farthings, “and not one of them is forgotten before God” (Luk 12:6–7). The argument is from the lesser to the greater: if the Father marks the fall of a worthless sparrow, how much more does He watch over His own children, for whom Christ died, whose very hairs are numbered. The sparrow also appears in the Psalms as a creature that finds her home in the courts of God: “Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts” (Psa 84:3), a sweet picture of the soul finding rest in the house of God. And the lonely sufferer cries, “I am as a sparrow alone upon the house top” (Psa 102:7), in his solitary grief. The sparrow thus preaches the meticulous, fatherly providence of God, who forgets not the least of His creatures and numbers the hairs of His children’s heads.
webster_summary: Small common birds of little market worth; our Lord’s emblem of the Father’s particular care, who marks each one and values His children far more.

corruption_summary: A creature-image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses the meticulous, fatherly providence of God over the least of His creatures and the great worth of His children.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the meticulous, fatherly providence of God. Our Lord chose the cheapest bird in the market, two sold for a farthing, to teach that not one of them falls to the ground without the Father, and not one is forgotten before God. If the Father marks the fall of a worthless sparrow, His children may rest assured that nothing befalls them apart from His will, for their very hairs are numbered, and they are of more value than many sparrows.

The sparrow rebukes both the fear that doubts God’s care and the deism that imagines God too great to mark small things. The God of Scripture is not a distant first cause but a present Father who numbers the hairs and notes the sparrow’s fall. And the sparrow that finds a house at the altars of the LORD pictures the soul that finds its rest and home in the presence of God; while the lonely sparrow on the housetop reminds us that even in solitary grief the Father’s eye is upon His own.
